sources.title: Grokipedia
sources.note: Not used; the standards documents were read directly. Facts in line texts that no standard states (dates, names of discoverers, numbers like 23.5 degrees) are flagged 'usual name' or are common textbook facts the quiz writers must still fact-check per the bank pipeline.

lines.text: Physical properties of matter, observed and measured: mass, magnetism, relative density (sinks or floats, with water as the reference), physical state (solid, liquid, gas), volume, solubility in water, and whether it conducts or insulates heat and electricity; other describing properties (colour, hardness, how it reflects light); identifying a material by its properties. Mass (amount of matter) and weight (gravity's pull) are both introduced, but the difference is not tested at this grade.

Matter is made of particles too small to see: evidence such as air filling and shaping a balloon, a scent (the smell of a rose) reaching us though we see nothing, a dissolved solid still present in water; 'atom' used only as a name for these tiny particles.
lines.placement_note: CK2010: G5 teaches atomic structure (nucleus, protons, neutrons, electrons in shells), elements, symbols and the periodic table. CK2019/2023: G5 keeps only invisible particles, 'atom' introductory. NGSS: G5 particles only; atoms and molecules 6-8 (MS-PS1-1, valence electrons excluded); atomic structure HS. TEKS 2021: G5 particles; elements and compounds G7; atomic structure only in IPC. Recommend G5 = invisible particles only; atoms and formulas at G7; protons, neutrons and electrons at G9.

lines.text: Mixtures, solutions and conservation of matter: in a mixture each substance keeps its own properties and can be separated (iron filings pulled from sand with a magnet; sand filtered or settled out of water); a dissolved solid makes a solution whose properties differ from its parts, yet nothing is lost; the total weight of matter stays the same through heating, cooling, mixing and dissolving; some mixings make a new substance (the first, unnamed look at chemical change).
standards: CK2010 G5 Chemistry: Matter and Change
lines.placement_note: Physical vs chemical change. CK2010: G5 (rusting iron, burning wood, milk turning sour vs cutting wood, breaking glass, freezing water). NGSS: G5 asks whether mixing makes a new substance (5-PS1-4); signs of reaction 6-8 (MS-PS1-2). TEKS: signs of chemical change G6 (6.6E); the named distinction G7 (7.6C). Recommend G5 asks only 'new substance or not?'; the signs at G6; the named physical/chemical distinction at G7.
lines.lane_note: Kitchen mixtures and dissolving (salad dressing, sugar in drinks, baking) belong to the cooking bank; use lab, rock and nature examples.

lines.text: Forces and motion: equal (balanced) forces leave an object's motion unchanged; unequal (unbalanced) forces start, stop, speed up, slow down or turn it and transfer energy; testing a force's effect with a car on a ramp or a balloon rocket on a string; Earth's gravity pulls objects 'down', meaning toward the centre of the round Earth.
lines.placement_note: Gravity: NGSS G5 (5-PS2-1, gravity points toward Earth's centre) and CK2023 G5 (Astronomy: Space Systems); TEKS 2021 first names gravity among forces at G6 (6.7A). Recommend G5 for 'gravity pulls toward Earth's centre'; G6 for gravity among named forces with net force.

lines.text: Energy changes form inside a system: a flashlight turns the battery's chemical energy into electrical energy and then light (and some heat); other everyday chains such as electrical energy to motion in a fan or to sound in a speaker.
standards: CK2023 G4 Energy Transfer and Transformation
lines.placement_note: CK2023 teaches energy transfer and transformation at G4; TEKS at G5 (NGSS grade-4 PEs not read). Recommend G5 (TEKS); kinetic and potential energy by name at G6.

lines.text: Electric circuits: a working circuit needs a complete, closed loop of an energy source (battery), conductors (wires) and a device; an open switch or a break stops the current; electrical energy becomes motion (motor), light (bulb), sound (buzzer) or thermal energy (heater); conductors (metals) vs insulators (plastic, rubber, glass).
lines.placement_note: CK2023 places electricity and magnetism at G2 (domain title only read); TEKS at G5; series and parallel circuits at G9 (TEKS IPC 6A). Recommend G5 for the simple circuit.

lines.text: Light's three behaviours: light travels in straight lines (sharp shadows, a laser pointer's beam); it is reflected (mirrors), refracted, or bent when passing between materials (lenses, a prism, a straw that looks broken in water), or absorbed (a dark surface warming in sunlight).
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G5. CK2023: G6 (Light and Matter). NGSS: reflected, absorbed or transmitted waves in 6-8 (MS-PS4-2). Recommend G5 for the three behaviours (TEKS); wave properties and the electromagnetic spectrum at G8.

lines.text: Ecosystems: organisms survive by interacting with biotic factors (other living things: food, predators, partners) and abiotic factors (sunlight, water, temperature, soil, air); what makes an ecosystem healthy; human activities that harm it (pollution, habitat loss) or help it (protection, restoration).
standards: CK2023 G5 Energy and Matter in Ecosystems

lines.text: Food webs: producers make food using sunlight; consumers (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores) eat; decomposers (bacteria, fungi) return matter to soil and air; energy flows one way from the Sun while matter cycles; the energy in an animal's food was once sunlight; predicting what happens to a web when one member grows, shrinks or disappears. (Trophic levels and energy pyramids are G7.)
standards: CK2023 G5 Energy and Matter in Ecosystems

lines.text: Plants make their own food: a plant's matter comes mostly from air (carbon dioxide) and water, not from soil; leaves use the Sun's energy and green chlorophyll to make sugar (glucose) and give off oxygen (photosynthesis: 'photo' = light, 'synthesis' = putting together); roots take in water; stems carry water (xylem) and sugar (phloem); tiny leaf pores (stomata) let gases in and out.
standards: CK2010 G5 Plant Structures and Processes
CK2023 G5 Energy and Matter in Ecosystems
lines.placement_note: NGSS (5-LS1-1) and CK2010 teach this at G5. TEKS 2021 names photosynthesis only as an energy transformation at G6 (6.8B), its chemical equation at G8 (8.6E), plant transport in Biology (Bio 12B). Recommend G5 for the core idea and the plant parts; the equation at G8.

lines.text: Structures that fit a place: how different species' body parts and features (beaks, teeth, roots, coverings, colouring) let each survive in the same environment; adaptations as inherited features that suit a habitat.
standards: CK2023 G4 Structures and Functions of Living Things
lines.placement_note: CK2023 teaches structure and function at G4; TEKS at G5. Recommend G5.
lines.lane_note: General adaptation science is ours; one named animal's anatomy for its own sake (the camel's hump, the giraffe's neck) is the animal bank's.

lines.text: Instinctive vs learned behaviour: instincts are inborn and need no teaching (sea-turtle hatchlings heading for the sea); learned behaviours come from experience or teaching (orcas learning to hunt in packs); both raise the chance of survival.
lines.lane_note: The TEKS examples are animal-bank material; the science question is only 'inborn or learned, and how does it help survival?'.

lines.text: Earth's rotation: Earth spins on its axis about once every 24 hours, causing day and night, the Sun's apparent path across the sky (rising in the east, setting in the west), and shadows that change length and direction through the day (longest morning and evening, shortest near midday).

The Sun is a star: it looks larger and brighter than other stars only because it is much closer; a star's apparent brightness depends on its distance; the star patterns (constellations) seen at night change with the seasons as Earth orbits the Sun.
lines.placement_note: NGSS and CK2023 teach this at G5; TEKS 2021 treats the Sun only as a member of the solar system at G7 (7.9A) and stars as such first at G8 (8.9A, life cycles and the H-R diagram). Recommend G5 for 'the Sun is a nearby star'; kinds and life cycles of stars at G8.

lines.text: The water cycle and where Earth's water is: the Sun's energy evaporates water (mostly from the ocean); the vapour rises, cools and condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation, and collects as runoff, lakes, groundwater and ocean; the Sun and ocean together drive weather; nearly all Earth's water is salt water in the ocean, and most fresh water is frozen in ice caps and glaciers or held underground.
standards: CK2023 G6 Weather, Climate, and Water Cycling
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G5. NGSS: water's distribution at G5 (5-ESS2-2); the cycle driven by sunlight and gravity in 6-8 (MS-ESS2-4). CK2023: G6. Recommend G5 for the stages and the distribution; G8 adds what drives weather and climate.

lines.text: Sedimentary rock and fossil fuels: weathering breaks rock into sediment; water and wind carry and drop it in layers; burial compacts and cements the layers into sedimentary rock (sandstone, shale, limestone), which holds most fossils; coal, oil and natural gas formed over millions of years from buried remains of ancient plants and sea life under heat and pressure. (All three rock types and the rock cycle are G6.)

Wind, water and ice shape the land: weathering, erosion and deposition build and carve landforms such as deltas (river sediment dropped at the mouth), canyons (cut by rivers over long time), sand dunes (heaped by wind) and glacier-carved valleys.
standards: CK2023 G4 Processes That Shape Earth
lines.placement_note: CK2023 teaches the processes that shape Earth at G4; TEKS at G5. Recommend G5.
lines.lane_note: Named landforms (the Grand Canyon, the Nile Delta, the Sahara's dunes) are the geography bank's; the processes are ours.

lines.text: Using and protecting natural resources: resources people take from Earth (water, soil, minerals, fuels, forests); renewable vs nonrenewable; reducing harm by conservation (using less), reuse and recycling, and proper disposal; how communities use science to protect land, water and air.
standards: CK2023 G4 Using Natural Resources for Energy

lines.text: Tools and metric units: what each tool measures and in what unit: metric ruler and metre stick (length, cm and m), balance and digital scale (mass, g), spring scale (force), graduated cylinder and beaker (volume, mL), Celsius thermometer (temperature, °C), timer (time); tools for seeing (hand lens, microscope, mirrors, prisms, concave and convex lenses); safe lab practice and safety equipment.
standards: NGSS NOS 3-5 Scientific Knowledge is Based on Empirical Evidence

lines.text: The fair test: ask a testable question; change only one thing (the variable being tested) and keep everything else the same; measure the result; repeat the trials; descriptive investigations (observing) vs simple experiments (testing); engineering: define a problem with criteria and constraints, compare possible solutions, find a prototype's failure points.
standards: NGSS SEP 3-5 Planning and Carrying Out Investigations

lines.text: Recording data and using models: tables, bar and line graphs, Venn diagrams, flow charts and cause-and-effect tables; finding patterns and sources of error in data; models (drawings, globes, a car-on-a-ramp set-up) and what each shows or gets wrong (size, scale, properties, materials).
standards: NGSS SEP 3-5 Analyzing and Interpreting Data
NGSS SEP 3-5 Developing and Using Models
lines.lane_note: Graph arithmetic itself is the math bank's; science questions ask what the pattern means.

lines.text: How science knows (grades 3-5 level): science answers only questions that evidence can settle; findings rest on patterns in observations; explanations can change when new evidence arrives; a scientific theory rests on a body of evidence and many tests; claims need evidence and are argued respectfully; discoveries and inventions change society.
standards: NGSS NOS 3-5 Science Addresses Questions About the Natural and Material World
NGSS NOS 3-5 Scientific Knowledge is Open to Revision in Light of New Evidence
NGSS NOS 3-5 Science Models, Laws, Mechanisms, and Theories Explain Natural Phenomena

lines.text: Science biographies (Core Knowledge grade 5): Galileo Galilei, 'father of modern science', whose telescope observations gave evidence for Copernicus's Sun-centred universe; Percy Lavon Julian, who developed synthetic cortisone to treat arthritis pain (CK calls him a biologist and inventor; he is usually described as a research chemist); Ernest Everett Just, biologist and medical pioneer who studied cells and reproduction in marine animals.
lines.placement_note: CK2010 G5 also lists Carl Linnaeus; this map moves him to G7 with taxonomy (TEKS 7.14A). CK2023 keeps a G5 Science Biographies domain, but its names were not readable (full 2023 PDF too large); CKSci's Science in Action pages feature living young scientists instead.
lines.lane_note: Galileo's trial and quarrel with the Church is the history (and theology) bank's; his observations and what they showed are ours.

lines.text: The solar system's eight planets in order from the Sun, the inner rocky and outer giant planets, and each planet's best-known feature (Mercury closest, Venus hottest, Jupiter largest, Saturn's bright rings, Mars red); the Moon orbits Earth and shines by reflected sunlight; Pluto a dwarf planet.
standards: CK2023 G3 Astronomy: Our Solar System
lines.placement_note: Added by the build lead, 2026-11-25, to place a topic where the approved plan's examples and the usual US course sequence put it; the 2017 TEKS teach the planets and their order at G3 (3.8D) and the 2021 TEKS place the solar system's members at G7 (7.9A, now G7.E1). The plan's own T1 example (Brandon, 2026-11-25) is 'Which planet is closest to the Sun?'. G5 here is the review of the basics every 10-year-old should know; G7.E1 goes on to comets, meteors, the Kuiper belt and gas vs ice giants.

lines.text: The body's main organs and their jobs: the heart pumps blood, the lungs take in oxygen and give off carbon dioxide, the stomach and intestines break down food, the brain and nerves carry signals, bones support and protect, muscles move the bones, the skin covers and protects.
standards: CK2023 G4 The Human Body: Our Circulatory & Respiratory Systems
lines.placement_note: Added by the build lead, 2026-11-25, to place a topic where the approved plan's examples and the usual US course sequence put it; Core Knowledge teaches the circulatory and respiratory systems at G4 and the body again at G5; TEKS 2021 and NGSS teach the systems as systems in 6-8 (G7.L3, G7.L4). The 2026-11-16 audit named body systems among the missing basics. G5 keeps to the organs and their jobs; G7 teaches the systems and how they work together.
lines.lane_note: Keep it clinical; no reproductive system at G5.

lines.text: Weather and climate, the basics: weather is the state of the air at a place and time (temperature, precipitation, wind, cloud cover, humidity); climate is a place's usual weather over many years; the tools that measure weather (thermometer, rain gauge, wind vane, anemometer, barometer); clouds are tiny droplets of condensed water, and the main kinds (cumulus, stratus, cirrus).
standards: CK2023 G6 Weather, Climate, and Water Cycling
lines.placement_note: Added by the build lead, 2026-11-25: the 2017 TEKS asked 5th graders to tell weather from climate (5.8A) and NGSS teaches weather and climate patterns at G3; Core Knowledge 2023 at G6; the 2021 TEKS keep weather and climate for G8 (G8.E4). G5 takes the basic words and tools; G8 what drives weather and climate.
lines.lane_note: Named places' climates are the geography bank's.

lines.text: States of matter as particles: in a solid the particles are packed tight and vibrate in place (fixed shape and volume); in a liquid they slide past one another (fixed volume, takes the container's shape); in a gas they move fast and far apart (fills any container); particle kinetic energy rises from solid to liquid to gas.

Pure substances vs mixtures: a pure substance (an element or a compound) has fixed properties; a homogeneous mixture or solution (salt water, air, brass) is the same throughout; a heterogeneous mixture (granite, sand in water) has parts you can see; physical properties such as melting and boiling point, density, magnetism and solubility tell them apart and let mixtures be separated.

Sorting the elements on the periodic table: each element has a one- or two-letter symbol (H, He, C, N, O, Na, Al, Si, Cl, Fe, Ag, Au); metals (most of the elements; CK2010 says about two-thirds, a dated figure to re-check: shiny, malleable, ductile, conduct heat and electricity) on the left and middle, nonmetals on the right (dull, brittle, poor conductors), metalloids along the staircase between (silicon: some of each); rare earth elements and why modern life needs them (strong magnets, electronics, batteries).
standards: CK2010 G5 Chemistry: Matter and Change
lines.placement_note: CK2010: G5 (elements, symbols, the periodic table, metals and nonmetals). TEKS: G6 (metals, nonmetals, metalloids, rare earth elements). NGSS: the table as a predictive model only at HS (HS-PS1-1). Recommend G6 for sorting elements by properties; G9 for the table's patterns explained by electrons.
lines.lane_note: Who mines, trades or controls rare earths is the economics or history bank's; the elements and their properties are ours.

lines.text: Density across fluids: density is how much mass is packed into a given volume; an object floats in a fluid denser than itself and sinks in one less dense; liquids of different densities stack in layers (oil on water); an egg or a person floats more easily in salt water than in fresh water. (The 2021 TEKS ask for comparison, not the D = m/V calculation.)
lines.lane_note: Any density arithmetic is the math bank's.

lines.text: Signs that a new substance has formed (possible chemical change): a gas produced (bubbles without boiling), a change in thermal energy (it gets hot or cold on its own), a precipitate (a solid appearing in a liquid), a colour change; these are evidence, not proof.
standards: CK2010 G5 Chemistry: Matter and Change
CK2023 G7 Chemical Reactions and Matter
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G6. NGSS: 6-8 (MS-PS1-2, properties before and after). CK2010: G5. CK2023: G7 (Chemical Reactions and Matter). Recommend G6 (TEKS).
lines.lane_note: Chemical changes in cooking (browning, baking, caramelising) are the cooking bank's.

lines.text: Forces around us: gravity, friction, magnetism, applied forces and the normal force (a surface pushing back); drawing force diagrams; adding forces along one line to find the net force; balanced forces (net force zero, no change in motion) vs unbalanced forces.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G6. CK2023: G8 (Contact Forces). NGSS: 6-8. Recommend G6.
lines.lane_note: The arithmetic of net force is the math bank's; science asks which way and what happens.

lines.text: Newton's Third Law: forces come in pairs; when one object pushes or pulls another, the second pushes or pulls back equally hard in the opposite direction at the same moment (a swimmer pushing water back, a rocket's exhaust, a book pressing on a table); the two forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G6. CK2023: G8 (Contact Forces). NGSS: 6-8 (MS-PS2-1, colliding objects). Recommend G6; the three laws together at G8.

lines.text: Kinetic and potential energy, and energy conservation: kinetic energy is energy of motion; potential energy is stored: gravitational (height), elastic (stretched or squeezed), chemical (food, fuel, batteries); energy is never created or destroyed, only transferred and transformed (a roller coaster trading height for speed; an electric circuit; a food web; photosynthesis storing sunlight).
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G6. CK2023: G8 (Contact Forces carries the kinetic-energy PEs in the OpenSciEd unit map). NGSS: 6-8. Recommend G6.

lines.text: Waves carry energy, not matter: transverse waves, where the medium moves at right angles to the wave (a rope wave; light and the other electromagnetic waves), vs longitudinal or compression waves, where it moves back and forth along the wave (sound, a pushed spring); crest and trough, compression and rarefaction.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G6. CK2023: G8 (Sound Waves). NGSS: 6-8. Recommend G6 for the two kinds; amplitude, frequency, wavelength and the electromagnetic spectrum at G8.

lines.text: Cell theory and how it was built: all organisms are made of one or more cells; the cell is the basic unit of structure and function; cells come only from existing cells. Its history runs through the microscope: Robert Hooke naming 'cells' in cork, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek seeing living 'animalcules', Matthias Schleiden (plants) and Theodor Schwann (animals), Rudolf Virchow ('every cell from a cell'). TEKS requires the history but names no one; these are the usual names.
standards: CK2010 G5 Cells: Structures and Processes
lines.placement_note: TEKS: cell theory G6, organelle functions G8 (8.13A). CK2010: G5 (cells and their parts). CK2023: G6 (Cells and Systems). NGSS: 6-8 (MS-LS1-1, -2). Recommend G6 for cell theory and its discoverers (TEKS and CK2023 agree); the organelles at G8 (TEKS).

lines.text: Kinds of organisms by their cells and food: prokaryotes (no nucleus: bacteria) vs eukaryotes (a nucleus: protists, fungi, plants, animals); unicellular (amoeba, paramecium, many algae) vs multicellular; autotrophs that make their own food (plants, algae) vs heterotrophs that take it in (animals, fungi).
standards: CK2010 G5 Cells: Structures and Processes
lines.placement_note: CK2010: G5 (cells without nuclei, single-celled organisms such as amoeba and some algae). TEKS: G6. NGSS: 6-8. Recommend G6.

lines.text: Variation within a population: members of one species differ (size, colour, resistance to disease, tolerance of heat or drought); when the environment changes, some variations help survival and others hurt it. (Natural selection by name is G7.)
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G6. NGSS: 6-8 (MS-LS4-4). CK2023: G8 (Natural Selection and Common Ancestry). Recommend G6 for variation and survival; natural selection named at G7 (TEKS 7.13D).

lines.text: Interdependence and competition: organisms and populations depend on, and compete for, biotic resources (food, mates, shelter) and abiotic ones (light, water, a temperature range, soil); a scarce (limiting) resource caps how large a population can grow.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G6. CK2023: G7 (Ecosystem Dynamics). NGSS: 6-8. Recommend G6.

lines.text: Relationships between species: predator and prey; competition; symbiosis in three forms: mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, the other is unaffected), parasitism (one benefits, the host is harmed).
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G6 (revisited for ecosystem stability in Bio 13A). CK2023: G7. NGSS: 6-8. Recommend G6.
lines.lane_note: Famous partner pairs (clownfish and anemone, oxpecker and rhino) are animal-bank stories; the three kinds of symbiosis are ours.

lines.text: Levels of ecological organisation: organism; population (one species in one area); community (all the populations living together); ecosystem (the community plus its nonliving surroundings).

Seasons: Earth's axis is tilted (about 23.5 degrees) and keeps pointing the same way as Earth orbits the Sun, so each hemisphere in turn gets more direct sunlight and longer days (summer) or slanting light and shorter days (winter); seasons are not caused by Earth's distance from the Sun; solstices and equinoxes.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G6. CK2023: G8 (Earth in Space). NGSS: 6-8 (MS-ESS1-1). Recommend G6.

lines.text: Tides: the Moon's gravity (and, less, the Sun's) raises bulges in the ocean, giving most coasts two high and two low tides a day; spring tides (largest range) when Sun, Moon and Earth line up at new and full moon; neap tides (smallest range) when they form a right angle at the quarter moons.

Moon phases and eclipses: the Moon shines by reflected sunlight; as it orbits Earth (about once a month) we see changing amounts of its lit half: new, crescent, first quarter, gibbous, full and back; a solar eclipse when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, a lunar eclipse when Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
standards: CK2023 G1 Sun, Moon, and Stars
lines.placement_note: NGSS: 6-8 (MS-ESS1-1, together with seasons). CK2023: G8 (Earth in Space; Sun, Moon, and Stars at G1). TEKS 2021 grades 5-8 do not list phases or eclipses (lower-grade TEKS not read). Recommend G6, beside tides and seasons, since all three come from the same Sun-Earth-Moon geometry.

lines.text: Earth's four spheres and their parts: geosphere (rock, soil, the interior), hydrosphere (oceans, rivers, lakes, ice, groundwater), atmosphere (the layer of gases around Earth), biosphere (all living things); how they act on one another (rain wearing down rock, plants changing the air, volcanoes adding gases).
lines.placement_note: NGSS: G5 (5-ESS2-1, the spheres interacting). CK2023: G5 (Modeling Earth's Systems). TEKS: G6 (6.10A). Recommend G6 (TEKS); the G5 water-cycle and rock lines already show the spheres interacting without naming them.

lines.text: Earth's layers: the crust (thin and solid; thicker continental crust, thinner oceanic crust), the mantle (hot rock that flows very slowly), the outer core (liquid iron and nickel) and the inner core (solid iron and nickel, the hottest part, kept solid by enormous pressure). (How we know, from seismic waves, is G9.)

The rock cycle: igneous rock forms when magma or lava cools (granite slowly underground with large crystals; basalt and obsidian fast at the surface); sedimentary rock from compacted, cemented sediment; metamorphic rock when heat and pressure change existing rock (limestone to marble, shale to slate); any rock can become any other through melting, weathering and erosion, or heat and pressure.
standards: CK2023 G6 Rock Cycling and Plate Tectonics

lines.text: Managing air, water, soil and energy: why resource management matters (cleaner air and water, enough food and energy for people); conservation, greater efficiency and new technology as the tools for managing them.
standards: CK2023 G7 Natural Resources and Human Impact
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G6 (watersheds and oceans at G7). CK2023: G7. NGSS: 6-8. Recommend G6.
lines.lane_note: TEKS 6.11A frames this through global energy poverty and malnutrition; prices, trade-offs and policy are the economics bank's (Bastiat voice). Keep this line to the science of pollution, efficiency and conservation.

lines.text: Hypothesis, theory and law: a hypothesis is a testable proposed explanation or prediction; a theory is a well-tested explanation supported by a large body of evidence gathered over time (cell theory, plate tectonics); a law describes a regular pattern in nature, often mathematically (Newton's laws of motion); 'theory' in science does not mean a guess.
standards: NGSS NOS 6-8 Science Models, Laws, Mechanisms, and Theories Explain Natural Phenomena

lines.text: Measuring like a scientist: SI units (metre, kilogram and gram, litre, second, degree Celsius); quantitative data (numbers) vs qualitative data (descriptions); repeated trials; mean, median, mode and range to describe data; sources of error and the limits of a data set.
standards: NGSS SEP 6-8 Analyzing and Interpreting Data
lines.lane_note: Computing a mean is the math bank's; science asks why trials are repeated and what the spread says.

lines.text: Weighing evidence and sources: judging a claim by the credibility, accuracy, cost-effectiveness and methods of its sources; cost-benefit analysis; how past and present research changed scientific thinking and society; science depends on evaluating proposed explanations, guided by values that keep measurements accurate and findings objective.
standards: NGSS NOS 6-8 Scientific Investigations Use a Variety of Methods

lines.text: The main parts of plant and animal cells and their jobs: cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, chloroplasts, cell wall and vacuoles; how plant and animal cells differ.
standards: CK2010 G5 Cells: Structures and Processes
lines.placement_note: Added by the build lead, 2026-11-25, to place a topic where the approved plan's examples and the usual US course sequence put it; Core Knowledge 2023 teaches the cell's parts at G6 (Cells and Systems) and NGSS in the 6-8 band (MS-LS1-2); TEKS 2021 waits until G8 (8.13A, G8.L1). The plan's own T2 example (approved 2026-11-25) is 'What part of a plant cell makes food from sunlight?'. So the basic parts and jobs sit at G6; G8.L1's line is then left without a unit of its own.

lines.text: The body's defences against germs: skin and mucus as barriers, stomach acid, white blood cells, fever, the lymph nodes, and the body's memory of a germ it has beaten.
standards: CK2023 G6 The Human Body: Circulatory, Lymphatic, and Immune Systems
lines.placement_note: Added by the build lead, 2026-11-25: Core Knowledge 2023 teaches the lymphatic and immune systems at G6; TEKS 2021 teaches all body systems together at G7 (G7.L3). The defences against germs sit at G6; G7.L3 keeps the supply systems.
lines.lane_note: No vaccines at G6 (the stance topic is T5).

lines.text: Elements, compounds and formulas: an element is made of one kind of atom (O, Fe, Au); a compound is two or more elements chemically joined in fixed proportions, with properties unlike its elements (H2O, NaCl, CO2); molecules; reading a formula with the periodic table: which atoms and how many of each (H2O is two hydrogen and one oxygen; C6H12O6 is glucose).
standards: CK2023 G7 Chemical Reactions and Matter
CK2010 G5 Chemistry: Matter and Change
lines.placement_note: CK2010: G5 (atoms, molecules, compounds; water H2O, salt NaCl, carbon dioxide CO2). CK2023: G7 (Chemical Reactions and Matter). NGSS: 6-8 (MS-PS1-1). TEKS: G7. Recommend G7.

lines.text: Physical vs chemical change: a physical change alters form or state but not the substance (cutting, breaking glass, freezing, melting, dissolving); a chemical change makes a new substance with new properties (rusting iron, burning wood, milk souring), judged by the G6 signs.
standards: CK2010 G5 Chemistry: Matter and Change
CK2023 G7 Chemical Reactions and Matter
lines.placement_note: CK2010: G5. NGSS: G5 introduction (5-PS1-4) and 6-8 (MS-PS1-2). CK2023: G7. TEKS: G7 (signs of change at G6). Recommend G7 for the named distinction (TEKS and CK2023 agree).
lines.lane_note: Cooking's physical and chemical changes are the cooking bank's; prefer metals, fire, rock and lab examples.

lines.text: Solutions in water: solute (what dissolves) and solvent (what does the dissolving; water dissolves so much it is called the universal solvent); concentration (how much solute in a given amount of solution) and dilution (adding more solvent); a solid dissolves faster with higher temperature, more surface area (crushed vs whole) and agitation (stirring or shaking).
lines.lane_note: Sugar in tea and other kitchen solutions are cooking-bank scenery; prefer ocean, body and lab examples.

lines.text: Speed and velocity: average speed equals total distance divided by total time; velocity adds direction (distance vs displacement); reading distance-time graphs (a steeper line means faster, a flat line means stopped).
lines.lane_note: The division itself is the math bank's; science questions ask what the numbers and slopes mean.

lines.text: Newton's First Law (inertia): an object at rest stays at rest, and a moving object keeps moving in a straight line at the same speed, unless an unbalanced force acts on it; why seat belts are needed, why a rolling ball stops (friction), why a quick tablecloth pull leaves the dishes. Isaac Newton is named in the grade's TEKS introduction.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G7. CK2023: G8 (Contact Forces). NGSS: 6-8. Recommend G7.

lines.text: How thermal energy moves: conduction (by contact: a metal railing hot in the sun), convection (by moving fluids: rising warm air, ocean currents, a pot of boiling water), radiation (by electromagnetic waves, even through empty space: sunlight, a fire's warmth); heat always flows from warmer to cooler until both reach thermal equilibrium; insulators slow it.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G7. CK2023: G6 (Thermal Energy). NGSS: 6-8. Recommend G7.

lines.text: Temperature and particle motion: temperature measures the average kinetic energy of a substance's particles (hotter means faster-moving particles); thermal energy is the total; adding or removing energy changes particle speed and can change the state.

Energy through trophic levels: producers, then primary, secondary and tertiary consumers; energy pyramids show the energy available shrinking at each level up, because most is used for living or lost as heat (the usual rule of thumb is about 10% passed on, a figure the standard does not state); why top predators are few; matter and nutrients recycle while energy flows through and out.
standards: CK2023 G7 Matter Cycling and Photosynthesis

lines.text: Levels of organisation in a body: cells form tissues (muscle, skin; in plants, bark or an onion's skin), tissues form organs (heart, stomach, brain; root, leaf, flower), organs work together as organ systems, in plants and in animals.
standards: CK2010 G5 Cells: Structures and Processes
lines.placement_note: CK2010: G5. CK2023: G6 (Cells and Systems). NGSS: 6-8. TEKS: G7. Recommend G7 (TEKS).

lines.text: Human body systems I, supply and defence: circulatory (heart, arteries, veins, capillaries, blood), respiratory (lungs, gas exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide), digestive (breaking food down, absorbing nutrients), urinary (kidneys filtering the blood), immune and lymphatic (white blood cells, lymph nodes fighting infection); how these systems work together.
standards: CK2023 G6 The Human Body: Circulatory, Lymphatic, and Immune Systems
CK2023 G4 The Human Body: Our Circulatory & Respiratory Systems
lines.placement_note: CK2023: circulatory and respiratory at G4; circulatory, lymphatic and immune at G6. NGSS: 6-8 (MS-LS1-3). TEKS: G7, all eleven systems together. Recommend G7 (TEKS).
lines.lane_note: Particular foods and diets are cooking-adjacent; keep to the organs and their jobs.

lines.text: Human body systems II, structure, control and reproduction: skeletal (support, protection, blood cells made in marrow), muscular (movement), integumentary (skin, hair, nails), nervous (brain, spinal cord, nerves; sense organs send signals to the brain), endocrine (glands release hormones: the pituitary at the base of the brain controls growth and other glands; the thyroid sets how fast the body uses food; the pancreas makes insulin, and too little causes diabetes; the adrenal glands release adrenaline in fear or anger), reproductive (producing offspring).
standards: CK2023 G5 The Human Body: Our Endocrine and Reproductive Systems
lines.placement_note: CK2010 and CK2023: endocrine and reproductive systems at G5, with the glands named. NGSS: 6-8. TEKS: G7 (the functions of all eleven systems). Recommend G7 (TEKS), using CK's named glands as the content.
lines.lane_note: Keep reproductive-system content clinical and brief (teen audience; nothing sexual).

lines.text: Reproduction and its results: asexual reproduction (one parent: bacteria splitting in two, yeast budding, spores of molds and mushrooms, strawberry runners and onion bulbs, regeneration) makes genetically identical offspring quickly; sexual reproduction (male and female gametes join: pollen and egg in flowers, leading to seed and fruit; cones in conifers; internal and external fertilisation in animals) makes varied offspring, which helps a population survive change; flower parts (sepal, petal, stamen and anther, pistil and ovary) and pollination by wind, insects and birds.
standards: CK2010 G5 Plant Structures and Processes
CK2010 G5 Life Cycles and Reproduction
lines.placement_note: CK2010: G5 (plant and animal reproduction in detail; CK2023 moved life cycles to G3). NGSS: 6-8 (MS-LS3-2, MS-LS1-4). TEKS: G7. Recommend G7, with CK2010's flower parts carried here.
lines.lane_note: One species' courtship or breeding habits are the animal bank's; the kinds of reproduction and their results are ours.

lines.text: Natural and artificial selection: in natural selection, individuals whose inherited traits suit the environment survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common over generations (Charles Darwin's idea; the standard names no one); in artificial selection people choose which plants and animals breed (crops from wild ancestors, livestock, dog breeds); newer technologies that shape inheritance (genetic modification, gene therapy).
standards: CK2023 G8 Natural Selection and Common Ancestry
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G7. CK2023: G8 (Natural Selection and Common Ancestry). NGSS: 6-8. Recommend G7 for the two kinds of selection; kinds of adaptation at G8; the full mechanism and evidence at G9.
lines.lane_note: Individual dog and livestock breeds are the animal bank's; crop domestication's story is history or cooking; the principle of selection is ours.

lines.text: Classifying living things: the ranks kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species; two-part scientific names in Latin form so scientists everywhere mean the same organism (Homo sapiens: genus capitalised, species not); taxonomists; Carl Linnaeus, botanist and 'father of taxonomy', who standardised the system; the recognised kingdoms and their roles (bacteria aid digestion, fungi decompose dead matter, plants produce food). Kingdom schemes differ by book (CK2010 used five: plant, animal, fungus, protist, moneran), and CK notes that DNA comparison has since reshaped classification.
lines.placement_note: CK2010: G5 (five kingdoms, the ranks, Linnaeus's biography). TEKS: G7. NGSS: no classification PE (relationships by common ancestry instead: MS-LS4-2, HS-LS4-1). Recommend G7 (TEKS), with Linnaeus's biography here.
lines.lane_note: Classifying one particular animal is the animal bank's; the system and why it exists are ours.

lines.text: Members of the solar system: the Sun; the four inner rocky planets and the four outer giants (gas giants Jupiter and Saturn, ice giants Uranus and Neptune); moons; asteroids (most in the belt between Mars and Jupiter); comets (icy bodies whose tails point away from the Sun); meteoroids, meteors (shooting stars) and meteorites; the Kuiper belt beyond Neptune (home of Pluto) and the far Oort cloud; their sizes, places and motions.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G7. CK2023: G8 (Earth in Space). NGSS: 6-8 (MS-ESS1-3, whose assessment boundary excludes recalling planet facts). Recommend G7.

lines.text: Gravity runs the solar system: the Sun's gravity holds the planets in orbit and planets hold their moons; gravitational pull grows with mass and weakens with distance; an orbit is a body's forward motion bent continually by gravity. (Kepler's laws are left out of the 6-8 band and come at G9.)

Why Earth can support life: its distance from the Sun lets water stay liquid (the 'habitable' or 'Goldilocks' zone); abundant water; an atmosphere with oxygen, a protective ozone layer and enough greenhouse warming to keep temperatures steady; compared with Venus (too hot) and Mars (too cold and thin-aired).

Evidence that Earth has changed: fossils (sea creatures' fossils high in mountains; fossils of the same land species on continents now oceans apart); superposition (in undisturbed rock layers the oldest lie at the bottom); evidence that continents move (coastlines that fit like puzzle pieces, matching rocks and mountain belts across oceans, features of the sea floor).
standards: CK2023 G6 Rock Cycling and Plate Tectonics
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G7. CK2023: G6 (Rock Cycling and Plate Tectonics). NGSS: 6-8. Recommend G7.

lines.text: Plate tectonics and what it builds: the crust and upper mantle are broken into plates moved by heat-driven currents in the mantle; at divergent boundaries plates spread (mid-ocean ridges, new ocean basins); at convergent boundaries they collide or one dives under the other (mountain ranges, deep trenches, volcanoes); at transform boundaries they slide past (earthquakes); hot spots build chains of volcanic islands; supervolcanoes.
standards: CK2023 G6 Rock Cycling and Plate Tectonics
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G7. CK2023: G6 (Rock Cycling and Plate Tectonics; Natural Hazards). NGSS: 6-8. Recommend G7.
lines.lane_note: Named volcanoes, ranges and island chains (Yellowstone, the Himalayas, Hawaii) are geography-bank scenery; the processes are ours.

lines.text: People and Earth's water: a watershed is all the land that drains into one river, lake or bay; groundwater (in aquifers) vs surface water; how farming, building, dams, pollution and conservation help or harm them; people depend on the ocean (food, climate, transport) and change it (overfishing, pollution, plastics).
standards: CK2023 G7 Natural Resources and Human Impact
lines.lane_note: Named rivers, seas and aquifers are the geography bank's.

lines.text: Designing a controlled experiment: the independent variable (what you change), the dependent variable (what you measure), controlled variables (what you keep the same), a control group to compare against; deciding which tools, how to record, and how many trials are needed to support a claim; descriptive, comparative and experimental investigations.
standards: NGSS SEP 6-8 Planning and Carrying Out Investigations
lines.placement_note: NGSS names independent and dependent variables and controls in the 6-8 band; the 2021 TEKS never name them, though their experimental investigations need them. Recommend G7, the middle of the band.

lines.text: Reading deep time: science assumes natural laws worked in the past as they do today; relative age (which layer or fossil is older, from superposition) vs absolute age in years; the geologic time scale (eons, eras, periods) built from rock layers and their fossils to organise Earth's roughly 4.6-billion-year history.
standards: NGSS NOS 6-8 Scientific Knowledge Assumes an Order and Consistency in Natural Systems
CK2023 G6 Rock Cycling and Plate Tectonics
lines.placement_note: NGSS: geologic time scale in 6-8 (MS-ESS1-4). TEKS 2021: superposition at G7 but no geologic time scale. CK2023: G6. Recommend G7 with superposition; dating rocks by radioactivity at G9 (HS-ESS1-6).

lines.text: Discovery story, from continental drift to plate tectonics: the jigsaw fit of continents and matching fossils led Alfred Wegener to propose continental drift (1912); most geologists rejected it because no force able to move continents was known; mid-twentieth-century mapping of the sea floor (mid-ocean ridges, magnetic stripes, Marie Tharp's maps) supplied the evidence, and plate tectonics became the accepted theory. Science explanations change with new evidence. (Usual names; the standards name no one.)
standards: NGSS NOS 6-8 Scientific Knowledge is Open to Revision in Light of New Evidence

lines.text: Mendel and inheritance: inherited vs acquired traits; Gregor Mendel's pea crosses (pure tall x pure short gave all tall, then about 3 tall to 1 short); dominant and recessive traits; one gene copy (allele) from each parent; genotype and phenotype; a one-trait Punnett square read in words.
standards: CK2010 G7 Cell Division and Genetics
lines.placement_note: Added by the build lead, 2026-11-25, to place a topic where the approved plan's examples and the usual US course sequence put it; the 2017 TEKS taught that genes on chromosomes govern inherited traits at G7 (7.14C); the 2021 TEKS moved genes and Punnett squares to G8 (8.13B, G8.L2); NGSS has Punnett squares in 6-8 (MS-LS3-2); the common 6-earth, 7-life, 8-physical middle-school sequence teaches Mendel in 7th-grade life science; the plan's own T3 example (approved) is Mendel's peas. G8.L2 then carries chromosomes, DNA and mutations.

lines.text: Sorting all matter with models: matter divides into pure substances (elements, compounds) and mixtures (homogeneous, heterogeneous); particle diagrams that show each kind (one kind of atom; atoms joined in fixed groups; different particles evenly mixed; different particles in clumps).

Chemical reactions conserve mass: reactants rearrange into products; atoms are neither made nor destroyed, so the mass before equals the mass after (even when a gas escapes an open container); reading a balanced chemical equation and counting the atoms on each side, with photosynthesis as the model (6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy -> C6H12O6 + 6O2); using the periodic table to identify the atoms involved; Antoine Lavoisier's careful weighing (usual name).
standards: CK2023 G7 Chemical Reactions and Matter
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G8. CK2023: G7 (Chemical Reactions and Matter). NGSS: 6-8 (MS-PS1-5). Recommend G8 for counting atoms in a given equation; balancing equations oneself at G9 (TEKS IPC 8B, NGSS HS-PS1-7).

lines.text: Water's special properties: cohesion (water molecules cling to one another: droplets, beading), adhesion (water clings to other surfaces: wetting, climbing narrow tubes), surface tension (a 'skin' strong enough to hold up a water strider or a carefully placed paper clip); together they help move water up through plants.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G8. NGSS: water's properties and their effect on Earth's materials at HS (HS-ESS2-5). Recommend G8.
lines.lane_note: The water strider as a creature is the animal bank's; here it is only evidence of surface tension.

lines.text: Acids and bases: the pH scale from 0 to 14 with pure water neutral at 7; acids below 7 (stomach acid, battery acid, acid rain), bases above 7 (soap, ammonia, bleach); the farther from 7, the stronger; indicators (litmus, pH paper) show which; an acid and a base can neutralise each other.
lines.lane_note: Kitchen acids and bases (vinegar, lemon juice, baking soda) are the cooking bank's; use body, soil, ocean and lab examples.

lines.text: Newton's Second Law: an object's acceleration depends on the net force on it and on its mass (force = mass x acceleration; force in newtons); the same push speeds a light object up more than a heavy one; a bigger net force gives a bigger acceleration.
lines.lane_note: Calculations are the math bank's; science asks how force, mass and acceleration trade off.

lines.text: Newton's three laws working together: seat belts and air bags (inertia; spreading a stop over more time), sports (kicks, catches, tackles), amusement-park rides, rocket launches (action and reaction), even the forces between colliding tectonic plates.

Describing waves: amplitude (wave height; the energy carried, heard as loudness), wavelength (crest to crest), frequency (waves per second, in hertz; heard as pitch, seen as colour); the electromagnetic spectrum from low to high frequency (radio, microwave, infrared, visible light from red to violet, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays), all travelling at the speed of light in empty space, while sound needs a medium to travel through.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G8. CK2023: G8 (Sound Waves; Electromagnetic Waves), with light at G6 (Light and Matter). NGSS: 6-8 (MS-PS4-1 leaves electromagnetic waves out of assessment), electromagnetic radiation at HS (HS-PS4-1, -3, -4). Recommend G8.

lines.text: Electromagnetic waves at work: radio and microwaves in wireless communication and microwave ovens; visible light through fibre optics; ultraviolet light to sterilise; X-rays to image bones; X-rays and gamma rays in radiation therapy for cancer; telescopes that observe the sky across the whole spectrum.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G8. NGSS: uses and effects of electromagnetic radiation at HS (HS-PS4-4, HS-PS4-5). Recommend G8.

lines.text: Forces at a distance: gravity, electric and magnetic forces act without touching, through fields; like charges and like poles repel, unlike ones attract; electric and magnetic forces grow with more charge or current and weaken with distance; an electric current in a coil makes an electromagnet; the pull of gravity depends on the masses involved.
standards: CK2023 G8 Forces at a Distance
lines.placement_note: TEKS 2021 grades 6-8 name magnetism only as one force (6.7A) and leave fields, charge and electromagnetism to IPC (5E, 6B). NGSS: 6-8 (MS-PS2-3, -5). CK2023: G8 (Forces at a Distance). Recommend G8 for the qualitative field picture (CK fills a TEKS gap); the force laws, circuits and induction at G9.

lines.text: The parts of a cell and their jobs: cell membrane (controls what enters and leaves), cell wall (rigid support in plants, fungi and bacteria), nucleus (holds the genetic material and directs the cell), cytoplasm (the jelly where the cell's work happens), ribosomes (build proteins), mitochondria (release energy from food), chloroplasts (photosynthesis, in plants and algae), vacuoles (storage; one large central vacuole in plant cells); plant vs animal cells.
standards: CK2010 G5 Cells: Structures and Processes
lines.placement_note: CK2010: G5 (membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, vacuoles, cell wall, chloroplasts). CK2023: G6 (Cells and Systems). NGSS: 6-8 (MS-LS1-2). TEKS: G8 (cell theory at G6). Recommend G8 (TEKS), keeping cell theory and the kinds of cells at G6.

lines.text: Genes and inheritance: chromosomes in the nucleus carry genes made of DNA; offspring receive one set of chromosomes from each parent; alleles, dominant and recessive traits, genotype vs phenotype; a one-trait Punnett square predicts the chances of each kind of offspring (Gregor Mendel's pea experiments; usual name); mutations, changes in genes, can be harmful, helpful or neutral.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: genes on chromosomes at G8; Punnett crosses (monohybrid and dihybrid, incomplete dominance, codominance, sex-linked traits, multiple alleles) in Biology (Bio 8B). NGSS: Punnett squares at 6-8 (MS-LS3-2 clarification). CK2023: G8 (Genetics). Recommend G8 for one-trait dominant/recessive crosses; G9 for the rest.

lines.text: Adaptations grow out of variation: inherited differences within a population lead, over generations, to structural adaptations (body parts, colouring, camouflage), behavioural ones (migration, hibernation) and physiological ones (venom, control of body temperature) that raise the chance of surviving and reproducing.
standards: CK2023 G8 Natural Selection and Common Ancestry
lines.lane_note: One species' adaptation (the camel's hump, the giraffe's neck) is the animal bank's; the three kinds and the process are ours.

lines.text: Disrupted food webs: how a population boom or crash, a natural disaster (fire, flood, drought) or human action (removing a predator, bringing in an invasive species, pollution) ripples through the transfer of energy in a food web.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G8. CK2023: G7 (Ecosystem Dynamics). NGSS: 6-8. Recommend G8.

lines.text: Ecological succession: primary succession on new, bare ground (cooled lava, rock left by a glacier) begins with pioneer species such as lichens and mosses that slowly build soil toward a stable community; secondary succession follows a disturbance that leaves the soil (a forest fire, an abandoned farm field) and goes faster; how populations and species diversity change along the way.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G8. CK2023: G7 (Ecosystem Dynamics). NGSS: 6-8 (MS-LS2-4) and HS (HS-LS2-6). Recommend G8.

lines.text: Biodiversity and stability: an ecosystem with many species and much genetic variety withstands and recovers from change better, and keeps providing services (clean water, pollination, fertile soil); losing biodiversity weakens it and the health of the organisms in it.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G8. CK2023: G7 (Ecosystem Dynamics). NGSS: 6-8. Recommend G8.

lines.text: The life cycles of stars: stars form in nebulae of gas and dust; a star's mass decides its path: Sun-like stars swell into red giants and end as white dwarfs; massive stars become red supergiants, explode as supernovae and leave neutron stars or black holes; the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram plots brightness (luminosity) against surface temperature or colour (red is cooler, blue hotter), placing most stars, the Sun among them, on the main sequence.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G8. NGSS: only distance and brightness at G5 (5-ESS1-1); stars' life spans and element-making at HS (HS-ESS1-1, -3). CK2023: the grade 5-8 domain titles show no stars domain after G5 Astronomy: Space Systems (bullets not read). Recommend G8 (TEKS).

lines.text: Galaxies: vast systems of billions of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity, sorted by shape into spiral, elliptical and irregular galaxies; the solar system lies in a spiral arm of the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy, far from its centre; Edwin Hubble's sorting of galaxy shapes (usual name).

The origin of the universe, from the data: distant galaxies are moving away from us (their light is shifted toward red), so the universe is expanding from a hot, dense beginning about 13.8 billion years ago (the Big Bang theory); the faint cosmic microwave background is radiation left over from it. TEKS words this as researching the data behind 'theories' of the universe's origin.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G8. NGSS: HS (HS-ESS1-2: light spectra, the motion of distant galaxies and the universe's composition as evidence). Recommend G8 for the theory and its two headline evidences; G9 for how spectra reveal composition and red shift.

lines.text: What drives weather and climate: weather is the state of the air from day to day, climate the long-run pattern of a place; the Sun's uneven heating (strong at the equator, weak at the poles), the oceans storing and carrying heat in their currents, and water vapour in the air together produce both. (G5 covered the water cycle; this is what powers it.)
standards: CK2023 G6 Weather, Climate, and Water Cycling
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G8. CK2023: G6 (Weather, Climate, and Water Cycling). NGSS: 6-8. Recommend G8.

lines.text: Global winds, air masses and fronts: unequal heating plus Earth's rotation (the Coriolis effect) produce global wind belts (trade winds, prevailing westerlies, polar easterlies) and jet streams that steer weather; air flows from high to low pressure; air masses (warm or cold, moist or dry) meet at fronts, where cold fronts bring short, sharp storms and warm fronts longer, gentler rain; forecasts are probabilities.
standards: CK2023 G6 Weather, Climate, and Water Cycling
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G8 (global air patterns and local weather; air masses named in 8.10C). NGSS: 6-8 (MS-ESS2-5 air masses and pressure; MS-ESS2-6 the Coriolis effect and prevailing winds). CK2023: G6. Recommend G8.

lines.text: Tropical cyclones: warm ocean water (roughly 26 °C and up) feeds rising, moist air; where ocean currents and air masses interact, storms organise and spin up into tropical cyclones, called hurricanes in the Atlantic and eastern Pacific and typhoons in the western Pacific; the eye, the eyewall and storm surge.
lines.lane_note: Named storms and their human stories (Katrina, the 1900 Galveston hurricane) are the history and geography banks'; how storms form is ours.

lines.text: What changes climate, from the evidence: natural causes (volcanic eruptions whose ash and gases cool the planet, meteor impacts, abrupt shifts in ocean currents, the release and absorption of greenhouse gases); human causes (burning fuels that release greenhouse gases, deforestation, urbanisation and city heat islands); the greenhouse effect itself (carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour trap outgoing heat).
standards: CK2023 G6 Weather, Climate, and Water Cycling
CK2023 G7 Natural Resources and Human Impact
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G8. NGSS: 6-8 (MS-ESS3-5) and HS (HS-ESS2-4, HS-ESS3-5). CK2023: touched by the G6 weather-and-climate and G7 human-impact domains (bullets not read). Recommend G8.
lines.lane_note: What to do about climate (costs, laws, energy policy) is outside this lane: science says what can happen, not what should (NGSS NOS). Economics and history own policy; no policy verdicts here. TEKS asks for both natural and human causes; teach both by their evidence.

lines.text: The carbon cycle: carbon moves between the air (carbon dioxide), living things (taken in by photosynthesis, given back by respiration and decay), the oceans (dissolved, and locked in shells), and rocks and fossil fuels (stored for millions of years, released by burning and by volcanoes).
standards: CK2023 G7 Matter Cycling and Photosynthesis
lines.placement_note: TEKS: G8, and again in Biology with the nitrogen cycle. NGSS: HS (HS-ESS2-6, HS-LS2-5). CK2023: G7 (Matter Cycling and Photosynthesis). Recommend G8 for the stores and flows; G9 adds the nitrogen cycle and the effects of disrupting both.

lines.text: Thinking with data: correlation is not causation (two things rising together need not mean one causes the other); mean, median, mode and variability; linear vs non-linear patterns in graphs; measurement error, precision vs accuracy, and improving both with better tools and more trials.
standards: NGSS SEP 6-8 Analyzing and Interpreting Data
lines.lane_note: The statistics themselves are the math bank's; science asks what the data can and cannot show.

lines.text: Discovery stories behind the grade's laws and charts: Isaac Newton's three laws of motion (named in the standards); Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell, whose diagram of the stars the standard names; and the usual names for the grade's other topics, not named in the standards: Edwin Hubble (galaxies, the expanding universe), Gregor Mendel (pea-plant inheritance), Antoine Lavoisier (conservation of mass). (CK2023 has a grade-8 Science Biographies domain whose names could not be read.)
standards: NGSS NOS 6-8 Science is a Human Endeavor

lines.text: What science can and cannot settle: science explains what happens in nature from evidence, and can describe the consequences of choices, but does not make society's decisions; its knowledge is limited by human capacity, technology and materials; scientists examine anomalies rather than ignore them; the certainty and durability of findings vary, and explanations are revised in light of new evidence.
standards: NGSS NOS 6-8 Science Addresses Questions About the Natural and Material World
NGSS NOS 6-8 Scientific Knowledge is Open to Revision in Light of New Evidence
NGSS NOS 6-8 Scientific Knowledge Assumes an Order and Consistency in Natural Systems

lines.text: The structure of the atom and how it was found: protons, neutrons and electrons, their charges and places (a tiny, dense nucleus; electrons around it; mostly empty space); the atomic number decides the element; the models of J. J. Thomson (the electron), Ernest Rutherford (the gold-foil experiment and the nucleus), Niels Bohr (energy levels) and James Chadwick (the neutron).
lines.placement_note: Added by the build lead, 2026-11-25, to place a topic where the approved plan's examples and the usual US course sequence put it; the 2017 TEKS taught the atom's structure at G8 (8.5A); the 2021 TEKS moved it to IPC (G9.P7); NGSS teaches atoms in 6-8 and their inner structure in high school; the common 8th-grade physical-science course teaches the parts of the atom and its models; the plan's own T4 example (approved) is Rutherford's gold foil. G9.P7 then carries the periodic table's patterns and valence electrons.

lines.text: Clues to common ancestry: the fossil record's order (simpler forms in older rock), transitional fossils, and similar bones and early embryos in different animals as evidence that living things share ancestors.
standards: CK2023 G8 Natural Selection and Common Ancestry
lines.placement_note: Added by the build lead, 2026-11-25, to place a topic where the approved plan's examples and the usual US course sequence put it; NGSS (6-8) and Core Knowledge 2023 (G8) teach the fossil record and anatomical and embryological similarity in middle school; TEKS 2021 keeps homologies for Biology (G9.L5). G8 takes the fossil and anatomical evidence; G9.L5 the molecular evidence, biogeography and the rates of change.
lines.lane_note: A particular animal's anatomy for its own sake is the animal bank's; homology as evidence is ours.

lines.text: Motion and collisions: position, velocity and acceleration over time in tables and graphs; net force, mass and acceleration read from data (Newton's second law, one dimension); momentum (mass x velocity) and impulse: making a collision last longer lowers the force (crumple zones, air bags, helmets, padded phone cases); momentum is conserved when no outside force acts.
lines.lane_note: Graph and formula work is the math bank's; science asks what the slope or the impulse means.

lines.text: The four fundamental forces and nuclear energy: gravity, electromagnetism, the strong nuclear force (holds the nucleus together) and the weak nuclear force (behind some radioactive decay); fission (splitting heavy nuclei, as in nuclear power plants) and fusion (joining light nuclei, as in the Sun); mass-energy equivalence, E = mc² (Albert Einstein; usual name): a little mass becomes a great deal of energy; uses, benefits and risks of nuclear technology (power, medicine, waste).
lines.lane_note: Nuclear weapons' history and politics are the history bank's.

lines.text: The laws of gravitational and electric force: both weaken with the square of the distance (twice as far, one quarter the force); gravity grows with the masses (Newton's law of universal gravitation), electric force with the charges (Coulomb's law); gravity only attracts, while electric force attracts or repels.
lines.lane_note: Any calculation is the math bank's.

lines.text: Electricity and magnetism at work: series circuits (one path; one bulb out, all out) vs parallel circuits (separate branches, as in home and car wiring); current, voltage and resistance in words; an electric current makes a magnetic field (electromagnets, motors) and a changing magnetic field makes a current, so generators turn motion into electricity (electromagnetic induction; Michael Faraday is the usual name).
lines.placement_note: TEKS: simple circuits at G5; series and parallel circuits and generators in IPC. NGSS: electric and magnetic force factors at 6-8 (MS-PS2-3), current and magnetic fields at HS (HS-PS2-5). CK2023: G8 Forces at a Distance (bullets not read). Recommend G9 for circuits and induction; the field picture and electromagnets' existence at G8.

lines.text: Energy conservation and the flow of heat: in a closed system total energy stays the same while it changes form; thermal energy moves by conduction, convection and radiation in weather, in living things and in machines; heat spreads until energy is evenly shared (the second law of thermodynamics), so no machine turns all its energy into useful work.

Waves carrying energy and information: wave speed equals frequency x wavelength; interference (waves adding up or cancelling, as in noise-cancelling headphones), reflection (ultrasound, sonar, radar) and refraction (lenses, fibre optics) used in medicine, communication and research; wireless signals, ultraviolet light and microwaves passing through, or absorbed by, different materials; digital signals as a more reliable way to store and send information than analog ones.
lines.lane_note: How computers and AI use digital data is the AI bank's; the physics of the signal is ours.

lines.text: Inside the atom, and the periodic table's patterns: protons (positive) and neutrons (neutral) in the nucleus, electrons (negative) in energy levels around it; the atomic number counts protons; valence (outermost) electrons decide bonding and reactivity; patterns in the table: a group shares properties (very reactive alkali metals, unreactive noble gases) and properties change steadily across a period; Dmitri Mendeleev's table, which predicted undiscovered elements (usual name).
standards: CK2010 G5 Chemistry: Matter and Change
lines.placement_note: CK2010: G5 (nucleus, protons, neutrons, electrons in shells). NGSS: atoms and molecules at 6-8, but valence electrons excluded until HS (MS-PS1-1 boundary; HS-PS1-1). TEKS 2021: atomic structure only in IPC (7A). Recommend G9.

lines.text: Light from atoms: an electron jumps to a higher energy level when energised and gives off a photon of a set colour when it drops back; so each element has its own emission spectrum, a fingerprint used to identify elements (neon signs, firework colours, the makeup of stars); light behaves both as a wave and as a particle (wave-particle duality); Niels Bohr's energy levels (usual name).

Chemical reactions and their rates: evidence of a reaction (an acid fizzing on a metal, rusting and other oxidation, combustion, an acid neutralised by a base); balancing equations so atoms, and so mass, are conserved; reaction and dissolving rates rise with smaller particles (more surface area), stirring, higher temperature and higher concentration; how a substance's properties fit its uses (sunscreen, fuels, industrial materials).
lines.placement_note: Counting atoms in a given balanced equation is G8 (TEKS 8.6E; NGSS MS-PS1-5); balancing one oneself is IPC (8B) and NGSS HS (HS-PS1-7). Recommend G9 for balancing.
lines.lane_note: TEKS IPC 7C names cookware; cookware and kitchen reactions are the cooking bank's, so keep examples industrial, environmental and lab.

lines.text: The cell's molecules and boundary, and the virus that is not a cell: carbohydrates (quick energy, plant cell walls), lipids (membranes, stored energy), proteins (enzymes, structure, transport) and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA: information); prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells and the scientific explanations of how complex cells arose (endosymbiosis is the leading one; Lynn Margulis is the usual name); homeostasis through the membrane by diffusion, osmosis (water) and active transport; viruses as genetic material in a protein coat that copy themselves only inside a host cell, how they spread and cause disease, and why antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses.
lines.lane_note: Nutrition (carbs and fats in food) is cooking-adjacent; keep to what the molecules do in cells. Virus and disease units fall under the science bank's own voice rule on pathogens and vaccines.

lines.text: The cell cycle: interphase (the cell grows and copies its DNA), mitosis (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) and cytokinesis; models of DNA replication; how one fertilised egg becomes trillions of specialised cells by differentiation, steered by genes and by the environment; cancer as cell division escaping its controls.

From DNA to protein: DNA's nucleotides (a sugar, a phosphate and one of four bases, A, T, C, G), the double helix and base pairing (A with T, C with G); a gene's sequence becomes a protein through transcription (DNA to messenger RNA) and translation (RNA to protein at the ribosomes); mutations (substitutions, insertions, deletions) and why some matter; molecular tools: PCR copies DNA, gel electrophoresis sorts it by size, genetic engineering changes it; the discovery of the double helix (Rosalind Franklin's X-ray image, James Watson and Francis Crick; usual names); TEKS also asks for scientific explanations of DNA's origin (the RNA-world hypothesis is the usual one).
lines.lane_note: Arguments over genetically modified food or gene editing policy get no verdict; the techniques themselves are ours.

lines.text: Meiosis and patterns of inheritance: meiosis halves the chromosome number to make sperm and egg cells; crossing over and independent assortment shuffle genes, so siblings differ; Gregor Mendel's laws; monohybrid and dihybrid crosses; incomplete dominance (red and white snapdragons giving pink), codominance (AB blood type), sex-linked traits (red-green colour blindness, haemophilia), multiple alleles (the A, B and O blood-group alleles).

Evidence for common ancestry: the fossil record (including transitional forms); biogeography (related species on nearby lands, distinctive island species); homologies: anatomical (the same bones in a human arm, a bat's wing and a whale's flipper), molecular (shared DNA and protein sequences) and developmental (similar early embryos); scientific explanations for the fossil record's different rates of change: gradualism, abrupt appearance (the Cambrian explosion) and stasis (punctuated equilibrium; Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould are the usual names).
standards: CK2023 G8 Natural Selection and Common Ancestry
lines.placement_note: NGSS: fossil patterns, anatomical and embryological similarity at 6-8 (MS-LS4-1, -2, -3) and multiple lines of evidence at HS (HS-LS4-1). CK2023: G8 (Natural Selection and Common Ancestry). TEKS: fossils as evidence Earth changed at G7 (7.10A); homologies and biogeography only in Biology. Recommend G9 for the lines of evidence (TEKS), with fossils already met at G7.
lines.lane_note: A particular animal's anatomy for its own sake is the animal bank's; homology as evidence is ours.

lines.text: How evolution works: natural selection changes populations, not individuals; Darwin's conditions (with Alfred Russel Wallace; usual names): inherited variation, more offspring than can survive, and limited resources lead to differences in reproductive success; speciation, when separated populations change until they can no longer interbreed; other mechanisms: genetic drift (chance, strongest in small populations), gene flow (migration), mutation and genetic recombination.

Photosynthesis, cellular respiration and enzymes: photosynthesis stores light energy in glucose in the chloroplasts (6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2); cellular respiration releases it in the mitochondria (C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy, stored as ATP), each the reverse of the other, matter conserved in both; aerobic vs anaerobic respiration (fermentation); enzymes are proteins that speed reactions by lowering the energy needed to start them, each shaped for its substrate, and slowed or wrecked by heat or the wrong pH.
standards: CK2023 G7 Matter Cycling and Photosynthesis
lines.placement_note: Cellular respiration. NGSS: 6-8 (MS-LS1-7, food rearranged to release energy) and HS. CK2023: G7 (Metabolic Reactions). TEKS 2021: first in Biology (11A). Recommend G9 (TEKS) for respiration and enzymes; photosynthesis's equation is already at G8.
lines.lane_note: Fermentation in bread, yoghurt and brewing is the cooking bank's; the cellular process is ours.

lines.text: Systems working together: in animals, systems cooperate for regulation (nervous and endocrine control; feedback loops that hold temperature and blood sugar steady), nutrient absorption (digestive with circulatory), reproduction, and defence against injury or illness (skin, the immune system); in plants, for transport (xylem carries water up, phloem carries sugar), reproduction (flowers, seeds) and response (tropisms: growing toward light, roots following gravity).

What keeps an ecosystem stable: predation, parasitism, commensalism, mutualism and competition as balancing forces; carrying capacity and what limits it; how disrupting energy flow or matter cycling through trophic levels destabilises an ecosystem; the carbon and nitrogen cycles (nitrogen fixed from the air by bacteria in soil and root nodules, returned by decomposers) and what happens when people disrupt them (fertiliser run-off, burning fuels); how environmental change, including human activity, alters biodiversity and so stability.

The Sun as a fusion star, and stars as element-makers: hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium in the Sun's core, turning a little mass into energy that slowly works outward and reaches Earth as radiation; the Sun's life span (about halfway through some 10 billion years); sunspots, the 11-year sunspot cycle and solar flares ('space weather'); stars forge heavier elements during their lives and in supernovae, so the atoms in living things were made in stars (nucleosynthesis).
lines.placement_note: TEKS: star life cycles at G8 (8.9A), fusion named only in IPC (5D). NGSS: fusion, the Sun's life span and element-making at HS (HS-ESS1-1, -3). Recommend G9 for the physics of how stars shine and forge elements; the life-cycle stages stay at G8.

lines.text: The Big Bang read from light: spectra show what stars and interstellar gas are made of; light from distant galaxies is red-shifted, showing that they recede and the universe is expanding; the cosmic microwave background is the remnant radiation of the Big Bang; the ordinary matter of the universe, about three-quarters hydrogen and one-quarter helium, matches the theory's prediction.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: evidence for the universe's origin at G8 (8.9C). NGSS: HS (HS-ESS1-2). Recommend splitting: the theory and its headline evidence at G8; spectra, red shift and the hydrogen-helium composition at G9, where IPC teaches emission spectra.

lines.text: Orbits by law: Newton's law of gravitation predicts the orbits of planets, moons and human-made satellites; Johannes Kepler's laws: orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus, a planet moves fastest when nearest the Sun, and planets farther out take longer to go round.
lines.placement_note: NGSS leaves Kepler's laws out of the 6-8 band (MS-ESS1-2 boundary) and uses them at HS (HS-ESS1-4). TEKS: in high-school courses outside IPC and Biology (Physics, Astronomy; not read). Recommend G9.
lines.lane_note: Arithmetic of orbital periods is the math bank's.

lines.text: Inside Earth and its deep past: seismic waves map Earth's interior (S-waves cannot pass through the liquid outer core); heat-driven convection in the mantle drives the plates; ocean crust is youngest at mid-ocean ridges and older with distance from them (seafloor spreading), while continents are oldest at their ancient cores; radiometric dating of meteorites, Moon rocks and Earth's oldest minerals dates Earth and the solar system to about 4.6 billion years; impact craters record their violent youth.
lines.placement_note: TEKS: in the upper-grade Earth Systems Science course only (§112.49; not read). NGSS: HS. Recommend G9 as the grade's Earth strand, building on the G6 layers and the G7 plates.

lines.text: Earth's systems and climate: a change in one sphere feeds back on others (melting ice uncovers darker ground and sea that absorb more sunlight); climate shifts when the energy flowing in and out changes (the Sun's output, slow changes in Earth's orbit, volcanic ash, greenhouse gases); carbon cycles among ocean, air, rock and life; life and Earth changed together (early photosynthesisers filled the air with oxygen); reaction products that degrade water, soil and air quality and change the global climate.
lines.lane_note: Policy is outside this lane: no verdicts on what governments or people should do (NGSS NOS 9-12: science says what can happen, not what should).

lines.text: Energy resources and the human story: renewable sources (solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, biomass) vs nonrenewable ones (coal, oil, natural gas, nuclear fuel) weighed by evidence: advantages, disadvantages, effects on society and the environment; how the availability of resources, natural hazards and shifts in climate have shaped where and how people live.
lines.lane_note: Prices, subsidies and energy policy are the economics bank's (Bastiat voice); civilisations shaped by climate are history's. Keep to the physical trade-offs.

lines.text: What makes a claim scientific (high-school level): hypotheses are tentative, testable statements; theories are well-established, highly reliable explanations that can still change with new evidence; laws describe relationships among observed phenomena; theories do not with time become laws; several lines of evidence pointing to one explanation make it stronger; questions that cannot be tested lie outside science; science is one way of knowing, set apart by empirical standards, logical argument and sceptical review, and it tells what can happen, not what should.
standards: NGSS NOS 9-12 Science Models, Laws, Mechanisms, and Theories Explain Natural Phenomena
NGSS NOS 9-12 Science is a Way of Knowing
NGSS NOS 9-12 Science Addresses Questions About the Natural and Material World
lines.lane_note: Other ways of knowing (faith, philosophy) are the theology and philosophy banks'; this line only marks where science's own method stops.

lines.text: Designing and judging investigations: a directional hypothesis (what will happen to the dependent variable when the independent variable rises); confounding variables; how much data, how precise, how many trials; sample selection and measurement error as limits; cost, risk and time; safe and ethical conduct; analysing, evaluating and critiquing explanations by empirical evidence, logical reasoning and experimental or observational testing; scientific values: precision, open-mindedness, objectivity, scepticism, replicable results and honest reporting.
standards: NGSS SEP 9-12 Planning and Carrying Out Investigations
NGSS SEP 9-12 Analyzing and Interpreting Data
NGSS NOS 9-12 Scientific Investigations Use a Variety of Methods

lines.text: Discovery stories the 9th-grade courses carry. Named in the standards: Newton's law of gravitation and Coulomb's law (HS-PS2-4), Kepler's laws (HS-ESS1-4 boundary). Usual names for the courses' content, not named in the standards: Gregor Mendel (inheritance), Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace (natural selection), Rosalind Franklin, James Watson and Francis Crick (the double helix), Albert Einstein (E = mc²), Niels Bohr (energy levels), Dmitri Mendeleev (the periodic table), Edwin Hubble (the expanding universe), Michael Faraday (induction). TEKS asks for the contributions of diverse scientists related to the content.
standards: NGSS NOS 9-12 Science is a Human Endeavor
